1.4.2 Behavioural measures
To get a single net placement location estimate per trial and participant (net placement center), we calculated the circular mean of the positions of the placed mosquito nets (0–7 nets) per trial and participant. Angles were wrapped … to avoid …  Error is the absolute circular distance in degree(°) between the placement centre and the hidden-state target. As described above, the hidden-state target is the center of the von Mises distribution and thus contains no outcome noise, unlike the observed attack direction. Analyses of how net placement centers were updated across trials use the observed attack direction. To compare placements across the two color cues, each participant’s learned cue-2 offset was subtracted from cue-2 placements. The offset was estimated, per episode, as the difference between the circular mean placements for the two cues on regular trials from the fourth trial of the episode onward, and averaged across episodes.
Net placements around each event are indexed as follows. The event trial (t0) is the trial in which the mosquito nets were placed before observing that the direction of the mosquito attack has shifted. The net placement in the event trial thus reflects a pre-event baseline. The first net placement after the displaced mosquito attack is t+1. The first net placement after the next attack is t+2; it is the first net placement at which an oddball and an episode transition can be distinguished – for an oddball, the target angle at t0 equals the target angle at t+2; for an episode transition, the target angle at t+1 equals the target angle at t+2. The following placement is t+3. After a transition, error is computed relative to the target angle of the new latent state, and after an oddball relative to the unchanged target angle.
Net entropy is the Shannon entropy, in bits, of the net allocation of the 7 nets over the 32 positions. It is 0 bits when all nets are stacked on one position and 2.81 bits when they occupy seven different positions, so that higher values indicate a wider spread of net allocation within a single trial.

1.5 Statistical Analysis
Statistical analyses were conducted in Python (version) and R/RStudio (version).
Trial- and episode-level data were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models (LMM) fitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML) in lme4 and lmerTest, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Proportions (beta distribution) and binary outcomes (binomial distribution) were modelled with generalized linear mixed models in glmmTMB (ref), tested with Wald z-tests. Model terms are reported as Type III F-tests.
Instruction condition was entered in every model as an unordered factor with two orthogonal, sum-to-zero planned contrasts. The first compares participants told the structure with those not told it (C3 versus the mean of C1 and C2, weights −1/3, −1/3, 2/3); the second compares participants told that rules exist with those told nothing (C2 versus C1, weights −1/2, 1/2, 0). With this coding, all other terms of a model are evaluated as the unweighted mean over the three conditions. Condition differences are reported as contrasts of the estimated marginal means (emmeans package in RStudio; ref), which average over the covariates of a model. Model coefficients are reported instead for interactions of condition with trial-level predictors, where they equal the difference between the contrasted conditions in the effect of that predictor. Planned contrasts are reported unadjusted. All pairwise condition comparisons are reported with Holm correction.
Random effects followed the design of each model, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes for the within-participant predictors and, where events or episodes were nested within participants, random intercepts for these units. Where this structure produced a singular fit, it was reduced stepwise, first by removing the correlations between random effects and then by removing random slopes. The structure used is reported with each model.
For each model, pre-specified ‘main-interest’ terms (A and D, the questionnaire term of the across-condition form and the condition × questionnaire term of the moderation form; B, the event type × placement × questionnaire term and its interaction with condition; C, the questionnaire × prediction error, questionnaire × state error and condition × questionnaire × state error terms) were corrected for the five questionnaires with the Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery rate (FDR), separately for each term, and are reported as q. Simple slopes and planned contrasts derived from a model are reported unadjusted. All p-values are two-sided.
1.5.1. The Effect of the Level of Instruction on Task Behavior
The effects of instruction condition on net placement behavior were estimated with six models:
To examine how … / the effect of instruction condition on the net placement error relative to the hidden-state target, we estimated the model (M1):
log(|error| + 1) ∼ condition × (within-episode position + episode index) + cue + oddball on the preceding trial × condition + episode length + (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode),
which was fitted at trial level. Because oddball trials … they were excluded from this model (t+1), such that the error describes …  The model contained a random intercept for participant, random slopes for within-episode position and episode index, as well as a random intercept for episode within participant.
To examine the degree to which participants stacked multiple nets in a single location or distributed them across multiple locations within a trial, we estimated the circular variance (cv) of the (up to) 7 net positions as cv = 1 - R (cv {element} [0,1]), where R is the resultant length. The effect of instruction condition on circular variance of net positions per trial was modelled with a beta generalzed linear mixed model with logit link (M2):
beta(|error| + 1) ∼ condition × (within-episode position + episode index) + episode length + episode index + (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode),
which was fitted at trial level.
A beta mixed effects model was chosen because circular variance, the dependent variable, is a …..
Furthermore, we examined the magnitude of change of the placement centre from one trial to the next, and how this is modulated by instruction condition, the different types of event trials (oddballs, episode transitions and outcome omissions). The change of the placement centre (shift) was calculated as the circular distance between the cue-offset-corrected placement centres of consecutive trials. A constant of 0.001 was added to the shift estimate to prevent zeros. The model (M3):
log(shift + 0.001) ∼ condition + oddball + transition + omission on the preceding trial + condition × (oddball + transition) + within-episode position + episode index + number of oddballs so far in the episode + episode length + (1 + oddball + transition | participant) + (1 | participant:episode).
… the model comprises fixed effects of instruction condition and each event type, as well as an oddball–transition contrast per condition to examine whether the differential reactivity to oddball events versus the differential reactivity to episode transitions varies across conditions. Regular trials are the reference category.
Next, we examined whether participants transfer an episode transition shift observed in one cue to the second cue in the first trial in which the second cue occurs in the respective episode. This cross-cue transfer  was operationalized as the angular distance between two placements for the cue shown second in a new episode (|I_e|): its actual placement at its first appearance, and the placement expected had its previous placement been rotated by the episode’s 120° shift. The previous placement is the circular mean of the last three placements for that cue in the preceding episode, and |I_e| = 0° indicates complete transfer. The model (M4):
|I_e| ∼ condition × (episode index + transition direction) + number of trials of the first cue before the first trial of the second cue + (1 + episode index + that number | participant)
included … fixed effects … interaction contrasts … random effects … random slopes … and was fitted at episode level, with one estimate per episode and participant.
To examine how overall mosquito defense performance differed between instruction conditions and across the session, we fitted a binomial mixed model of whether a net intercepted the mosquito attack (M5):
intercepted ∼ condition × episode index + within-episode position + episode length + (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode).
… fixed effect of the level of instruction (condition), episode index, as well as their interaction, to test whether how mosquito defense performance varies across episodes differs between instruction conditions.   … random effects … random slopes …
The net placement error relative to the true hidden target at t0 to t+3 was modelled separately for episode transitions and oddballs, to investigate differences in net placement error patterns around the different events. An interaction effect between condition and trial (t0:t+3) operationalized how net placement error patterns around events differed across instruction conditions. The model (M6) was fitted as:
log(|error| + 1) ∼ condition × trial + (1 | participant) + (1 | participant:event),
with trial as a four-level factor (t0:t+3). Planned contrasts between conditions were computed at each placement.
Finally, we examined the effect of the level of instruction on the relative weighting of state error relative to outcome noise in trial-by-trial updating of mosquito net allocation centers. On each regular trial with an observed attack, the prediction error (observed mosquito attack direction – net placement centre) is the sum of two components known to the experimenter: the outcome noise (observed mosquito attack direction – hidden-state target) and the state error (hidden-state target – net placement centre). The change of the net placement centre from that trial to the next was modelled as (M7):
update ∼ condition × (prediction error + state error) + next-trial cue switch × (prediction error + state error) + (1 + prediction error + state error | participant).
In this parameterization, the coefficient of the prediction error is the weight on outcome noise, i.e. on the irreducible stochasticity, and thus the irreducible component of the total uncertainty. The coefficient of the state error is the additional weight on state error (distance of the net placement to the hidden-state target) beyond the weight on noise; the estimate is zero for a learner that responds to every outcome alike. All angles were expressed in the participant’s own frame (after removing the learned cue offset), and pairs in which the next trial showed either cue were included. Condition-specific additional weights were obtained as simple slopes with emtrends (ref), at pairs in which the next trial showed the same cue.
1.5.2 Models of the Questionnaire Score Associations
To examine how internalizing symptoms modulate overall task performance and signatures of structural inference, we estimated four linear mixed-effects-models (A–D) per questionnaire scale (trait anxiety [STICSA-T], state anxiety STICSA-S], depressive symptoms [BDI-II], intolerance of uncertainty [UI-18] and obsessive compulsive behavior [OCI-R]). Model A asks whether questionnaire scores relate to overall performance, as a boundary condition for the remaining models. Model B asks whether questionnaire scores relate to the response to an episode transition differently than to an oddball, that is, to a displaced attack that does or does not signal a change of latent state. Model C asks whether questionnaire scores relate to the weighting of state error (i.e. angular error between the participant’s current placement and the hidden target angle) relative to outcome noise. Model D asks whether questionnaire scores relate to the transfer of an episode transition to the second (i.e. previously unseen within the new episode) color cue. Each model was fitted separately for each of the five questionnaires.
Each model was fitted in two forms. First, we fitted the models across instruction conditions, with the model containing the questionnaire but no condition × questionnaire interaction, so that the questionnaire slope is estimated from all participants, each condition contributing in proportion to its size. These models are estimated to examine whether a questionnaire is associated with the outcome irrespective of instruction (i.e. which information about the hidden structure was provided). Second, we fitted an extended form of this model, by adding the condition × questionnaire interactions. From these models, the questionnaire slopes were estimated in each condition, pooled over C1 and C2 (participants not told the structure), and as the two planned contrasts between conditions. In these moderation-form models, the questionnaire main effect is the unweighted mean of the three condition-specific slopes, in which the (current) 13 C3 participants count as much as the (current) 29 C2 participants, and it is therefore not used as the across-condition estimate.
To examine whether questionnaire scores are associated with overall task performance (Model A), we extended  M1 and M5 by the questionnaire (A1, error relative to the hidden-state target, A2, interception), with the questionnaire term added to the fixed effects of M1 and M5 and the same random effects (A1, A2, (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode)).
Whether questionnaire scores are related to differences in response to oddballs compared to episode transitions was examined across the first (t+1) and second (t+2) post-event trial. For each episode transition and each oddball, the net placements in  t+1 and t+2 entered the model,
outcome ∼ condition × event type × trial × questionnaire + (1 + event type | participant) + (1 | participant:event),
with event type (oddball, transition) and placement (t+1, t+2) coded −1/2 and +1/2. The outcome was net placement error relative to the hidden-state target (B1) or net entropy (B2). The three-way interaction event type × trial × questionnaire tests whether the association of the questionnaire with the change of the outcome from t+1 to t+2 differs between episode transitions and oddballs. From the model, the questionnaire slope was estimated for each event type and placement, together with its change from t+1 to t+2 for each event type and the difference between event types at each placement.
In B2, the random slope for event type produced a singular fit and was removed. Because the three-way interaction term varies within participants, B1 was refitted as a sensitivity model with uncorrelated by-participant random slopes for event type, trial and their interaction (reduced to event type and event type × trial where singular). For B2, these random slopes were estimated at zero, so that the sensitivity model reproduced the primary model. MOVE THIS PARAGRAPH TO RESULTS?
Furthermore, we examined whether questionnaire scores modulated the relative weighting of state error (net placement error relative to the hidden state target) relative to outcome noise in trial-by-trial updating of mosquito net allocation centers, using the model (Model C)
update ∼ condition × (prediction error + state error) + questionnaire × prediction error + questionnaire × state error + condition × questionnaire × state error + next-trial cue switch × (prediction error + state error) + (1 | participant).
The questionnaire × prediction error term operationalized the effect of the questionnaire scores on the weight on outcome noise; the questionnaire × state error term operationalized the effect of questionnaire scores on the additional weight on state error. Condition-specific slopes of the additional weight on state error were computed as linear combinations of the fixed effects (lmerTest::contest). The model contains a by-participant random intercept; a sensitivity model added an uncorrelated by-participant random slope for the state error (see supplementary material, ADD).
An extended version of the cross-cue transfer model (M4) described above to examine whether questionnaire scores differentially modulated cross-cue transfer across instruction conditions. The model was estimated (Model D) as
|I_e| ∼ condition × questionnaire + number of first-cue trials × questionnaire + condition × (episode index + transition direction) + (1 + episode index + number of first-cue trials || participant),
with the number of first-cue trials centred on its mean. The random-effect correlations were removed because the correlated structure was singular. The interaction between the number of first-cue trials after an episode transition and questionnaire score additionally tested whether questionnaire scores are associated with differences in cross-cue transfer for different numbers of consecutive observations of the first color cue after an episode transition. To assess the influence of single participants on the slope in C3, the moderation form was refitted leaving out each of the 13 C3 participants with questionnaire data in turn. Participants thus responded to displaced mosquito attacks, and moved their net placement less after trials on which no mosquito attack had been shown (omission trials). With deeper instruction they moved more after episode transitions than after oddballs. The condition effects (level of instruction) on net placement error relative to the target angle (hidden-state target) after events was estimated with a linear mixed-effects model (M6), as planned contrasts of the condition means at each net placement. After episode transitions, the difference between conditions depended significantly on the trial (condition × trial F(6, 1618) = 15.48, p < .001) – on the transition trial itself (t0), placed before the first attack of the new latent state, net placement error did not differ significantly between conditions (C3 versus C1 + C2, 0.16 log units, SE = 0.139, t(235.9) = 1.16, p = .247; C2 versus C1, −0.08, SE = 0.127, t(236.6) = −0.65, p = .517). From the first net placement after the episode transition onward, net placement error was significantly lower in C3 than in C1 and C2, by an amount that increased across trials.

The model-estimated mean net placement error was 3.98 (C1), 3.80 (C2) and 3.14 (C3) log units at t+1, 3.53, 3.36 and 2.39 at t+2, and 3.82, 3.63 and 2.48 at t+3. Descriptively, the net placement center at t+1 had moved 0.24 (C1), 0.29 (C2) and 0.61 (C3) of the 120° rotation toward the new latent state, and at t+2 0.34, 0.37 and 0.79. In all conditions, net placement error rose again from t+2 to t+3. This rise coincides with the first appearance of the other color cue after the episode transition, which carries higher error than a repeat appearance of the first color cue (supplementary analysis ADD).

After oddballs, the difference between conditions did not depend significantly on the trial (condition × trial F(6, 2839) = 2.08, p = .052). Net placement error was lower in C3 than in C1 and C2 in every trial, including the oddball trial itself (t0, −0.81 log units, SE = 0.172, t(96.9) = −4.72, p < .001; t+1, −0.58, p = .001; t+2, −0.91, p < .001; t+3, −0.96, p < .001), and did not differ significantly between C2 and C1 in any trial (all p ≥ .093). Because oddballs occur within stable phases, in which C3 participants were more accurate, the C3 advantage after oddballs reflects their accuracy before the oddball rather than a different response to it.

2.1.5 Weighting of state (hidden target) error relative to outcome noise

children.label: 2.1.5 Weighting of state (hidden target) error relative to outcome noise

children.value: The additional weight on state error (updating based on the hidden state target) compared to weight on noise was estimated with the weighting model (M7) described above. Condition-specific weights were obtained as simple slopes, and condition differences as planned contrasts of those slopes.

The additional weight on state error did not differ significantly from zero in C1 (0.07, SE = 0.095, t(60.9) = 0.72, p = .476), and it was significantly greater than zero in C2 (0.25, SE = 0.088, t(43.2) = 2.80, p = .008) and in C3 (0.66, SE = 0.184, t(658.0) = 3.56, p < .001). It was significantly greater in C3 than in C1 and C2 (planned contrast = 0.50, SE = 0.188, t(386.3) = 2.65, p = .008), and it did not differ significantly between C2 and C1 (planned contrast = 0.18, SE = 0.118, t(41.8) = 1.52, p = .137).

The weight on outcome noise was significantly greater than zero in C1 (0.37, SE = 0.094, t(57.8) = 3.87, p < .001) and C2 (0.30, SE = 0.088, t(41.6) = 3.36, p = .002), but not in C3 (0.08, SE = 0.181, t(562.3) = 0.44, p = .663). The planned contrasts of the weight on outcome noise were not significant (C3 versus C1 + C2, −0.25, SE = 0.185, t(334.3) = −1.36, p = .176; C2 versus C1, −0.07, SE = 0.118, t(39.8) = −0.58, p = .564).

Expressed as percentages, participants in C1 followed on average 37% of the outcome noise and corrected 43% of the state error, participants in C2 followed 30% and corrected 54%, and participants in C3 followed 8% of the noise and corrected 73% of the state error. The weight on outcome noise thus decreased descriptively with instruction, but only the additional weight on state error differed significantly between participants told and not told the structure. Participants in C1 corrected their error about the hidden state no more than they followed outcome noise, whereas participants in C3 corrected state error selectively.

On net placement error, recovery after episode transitions, transfer to the second color cue and the weighting of state error relative to noise, the effect of instruction was predominantly carried by the planned contrast between C3 and the other two conditions. The contrast between C2 and C1 was not significant on any of these measures. Participants told the latent structure moved their net placement further after episode transitions than after oddballs, carried the change over to the second color cue more often, and corrected their estimate of the hidden state more selectively relative to outcome noise.

Trait anxiety and related constructs (as well as internalizing symptoms more broadly, see below) show no significant main-effect relationship with structural inference. Nonetheless, the descriptive effects build a coherent set of condition-dependent and transition-specific associations that converge across scales and analyses. The clearest is a large, uniformly-signed family of trait x instruction-depth interactions on cue-dissociation (IU-prospective β=−0.62, ERS −0.61, IU-total −0.55, plus EAT, IU-inhibitory, OCI same-signed), suggesting that the structural-generalization benefit of deeper instruction is systematically modulated by uncertainty-/internalizing-related traits, i.e. individual differences express themselves specifically where structure is manipulated. A second group of descriptive effects links (state/cognitive) anxiety to higher net-placement entropy (and lower stacking) (β≈+0.27). Interpreted cautiously, high anxiety individuals may thus infer higher local stochasiticity compared to individuals with low-to-medium anxiety. This converges with earlier evidence from tasks in which individuals learn to distinguish between volatility and stochasticity, where high trait anxiety was assocated with an overestimation of stochasticity and an underestimation of volatility (cite). Crucially, this was commonly interpreted as reduced or even affected learning (cite). Our results provide an alternative interpretation: while outcome variability within stable latent states is more readily attributed to stochastic noise, thereby decreasing sensitivity to volatility as long as this volatility does not arise from a specific hidden structure, reactivity to structured variablility of the generative structure itself (i.e. state transitions) is increased while sensitivity to stochasiticity at this structure-level is decreased. This is not consistent with generally altered/ reduced learning but with a different focus on

should be learned. It is further consistent with evidence demonstrating, that high anxiety individuals have a higher tendency to infer and rely on (hidden) structures in the context of latent state inference (Zika et al., 2023). A higher structural prior / more pronouced expectation that dynamics are driven by switches between discrete states rather than continuous gradual dynamics would give rise to a “misatribution” of volatility to stochasticity as long as the observed variablility through volatility is not distinguishable from local within-state stochasticity (actually a higher tolerance for local noise, in order to stick with model that provides a structured explanation for the observed dynamics, thereby allowing for straightforward action selection - otherwise, the uncertainty about the model generating outcomes would have to increase rapidly). But as soon as volatility is governed by a certain hidden structure that can be identified, this “misattribution” diminishes. Instead, high-anxiety/ internalizing idividuals show a relatively “better” structural inference compared to individuals with lower anxiety/internalizing symptom load.

This pattern of effects suggests that higher internalizing symptom load is associated with larger post-transition belief updates, stronger transition-recovery and a (marginally) higher structure-learning index. The sign is positive throughout, consistent with the hypothesis that anxiety may

structure learning. Moreover, this pattern is specifically about transitions (genuine structural change), not about oddballs (noise). For oddballs, the direction of the effect is reversed and weaker (oddball_reactivity x IU β=−0.23, x OCI −0.29), suggesting that higher internalizing symptom load is associated with less oddball reactivity. convergent-validity pairings hold for the well-recovered parameters: precision
weighting with net entropy (r = −0.87, p = 5 x 10⁻²²) and stacking (r = +0.62),
cue sensitivity with the learned cue offset (r = +0.81, p = 9 x 10⁻¹⁷), and
belief momentum with post-transition belief revision (r = −0.42, p = 4 x 10⁻⁴),
all Holm-significant within family.

The computational model is identifiable, calibrated and valid
against the behavioural measures it indexes, and it selects structural inference
over gradual tracking essentially unanimously.

No trait–parameter association survives FDR correction (yet?), and no mediation path
reaches significance, as expected when both constituent paths are of the order
r = 0.3 at N = 65.

Posterior predictive checks reproduce most behavioural signatures (spontaneous
switch rate 75% coverage; large-shift rate and oddball-follow rate approximately
68%), without a coverage area bias (the CIs are fairly tight, so that the absolute deviation remains practically negligible). Belief lability was not reproduced (16% coverage, observed exceeding
predicted in 57 of 68 participants), nor fully are within-state placement
variance and oddball angular shift (the latter two features are sufficiently close though).
The reason for this pattern is that the model cannot jump as fast as participants do - I’m still trying to find a solution for this but IMO even the current version captures participant behavior very well. These differences are genuinely really hard to recognize in the net placement heatmaps (participant behavior vs model behavior, replayed with the participant’s inferred parameters). Here a few examples:

Noise reactivity is the least identifiable parameter (recovery r = 0.64,
reliability ≈ 0.41). Diagnostic work established that this is a property of the
forward model rather than of the estimation method: an independent supervised
learner trained on the same summary features reproduces the recovery profile of
the neural estimator to two decimal places, and the parameter’s behavioural
channels are suppressed downstream (the learning gate saturates at κ = 4 with a
120° displacement, and the predictive mixture component is removed by the
commitment sharpening before net allocation). A two-stage allocation reserving
round(7 x ρ_eff) nets for the oddball location raises the ceiling from 0.60 to
0.92 in simulation, at a cost of 0.09 for perceived volatility, leaving switching
behaviour unchanged. The model has been patched and awaits retraining and
posterior predictive re-validation (just didn’t find the time yet - this is retraining No.9 (?) and the training has to run over night). Until then, results involving noise reactivity, including the absence of the predicted association with trait
anxiety, are limited by identifiability rather than evidence of absence.
Nevertheless, different noise reactivity values produce exactly the expected model behavior:

The transition-versus-oddball distinction is where the three questions come together. RQ1
establishes that instructed structure changes what is propagated across cues and
retained across trials, and that propagation scales with prior evidence. RQ3
establishes that the generative account is latent-state inference rather than
gradual tracking, and that belief momentum indexes post-transition revision. RQ2
places internalizing load on the same axis: larger post-transition updating,
lower oddball reactivity and lower belief momentum, observed consistently at the
behavioural, parameter and symptom levels, though no individual association is
resolved at the present sample size.
